\chapter{In the Kitchen}
\label{ch:hi-in-the-kitchen}
\hlchaptermodality{52}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five things in a Hindi kitchen and ask for them politely.}

Complete HI-C52-vegetable and say all five words in order.

\section[chāval]{\hi{चावल} (chāval) — rice}

\label{lesson:HI-C52-rice}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did the last two words of the chapter before mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{चावल}}
\textbf{\hi{चावल}} (\emph{chāval}) — \textquotedblleft{}rice\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit's own word for rice is \hi{तण्डुल} (\emph{taṇḍula}), and it is not the ancestor of this one. Where \emph{chāval} came from is genuinely unsettled — the dictionaries record the Prakrit forms behind it without agreeing on what stands behind those.

That makes it the fourth everyday Hindi word you have met whose origin is honestly unknown, after \hi{बिल्ली}, \hi{कुत्ता} and \hi{पेट}. It is worth noticing the pattern: the words a language uses most are not always the words whose history it kept.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things a kitchen is stocked with.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chāval}
  \item \emph{Say it:} it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chāval}, the grain the rest of the meal is served over
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ābhār}, then read \textbf{\hi{फूल}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{चावल} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}rice\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dāl]{\hi{दाल} (dāl) — lentils, split pulses}

\label{lesson:HI-C52-lentils}



\begin{quote}
What did the word before this one mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{दाल}}
\textbf{\hi{दाल}} (\emph{dāl}) — \textquotedblleft{}lentils, split pulses\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{दल्} (\emph{dal-}), 'to split', through the noun \hi{दल} (\emph{dala}), 'a piece torn off'. \hi{दाल} is not the name of a plant at all — it is the name of what was done to the seed.

Whole pulses are not \hi{दाल}; split ones are. So the word draws its line through the middle of the lentil rather than around the outside of the species, which is why one plant can give both a \hi{दाल} and a not-\hi{दाल}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The second of five, and the one named after a knife rather than a plant.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dāl}
  \item \emph{Say it:} it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{dāl}, then \emph{chāval} — the pair that makes a meal
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\hi{एहसान}}, then say \emph{mālā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{दाल} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}lentils, split pulses\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tel]{\hi{तेल} (tel) — oil}

\label{lesson:HI-C52-oil}



\begin{quote}
Name the 2 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{तेल}}
\textbf{\hi{तेल}} (\emph{tel}) — \textquotedblleft{}oil\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{तैल} (\emph{taila}), which is built on \hi{तिल} (\emph{tila}), 'sesame'. \hi{तेल} is therefore 'the sesame stuff' — oil named after the one seed that was pressed for it.

English did the same thing by a different road: \emph{oil} goes back to Latin \emph{oleum}, from Greek \emph{élaion}, 'olive oil' — oil named after the olive. Two languages, two plants, one habit of naming the substance after whatever you happened to press.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The third of five, and a word that still smells of one particular seed.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tel}
  \item \emph{Say it:} it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tel}, the thing the \hi{दाल} is finished with
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{ādar}, then read \textbf{\hi{आँगन}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{तेल} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}oil\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chīnī]{\hi{चीनी} (chīnī) — sugar}

\label{lesson:HI-C52-sugar}



\begin{quote}
Name the 3 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{चीनी}}
\textbf{\hi{चीनी}} (\emph{chīnī}) — \textquotedblleft{}sugar\textquotedblright{}.

\hi{चीनी} means, quite literally, 'Chinese'. The everyday Hindi word for sugar names the country the refining technique was associated with — the same shape as calling a thing \emph{china} because of where it was made.

The traffic ran the other way too. English \emph{sugar} came through Arabic \emph{sukkar} from Sanskrit \hi{शर्करा} (\emph{śarkarā}), 'grit, gravel' — so India exported the word for sugar to Europe and then named its own everyday sugar after China. Both halves of that are true at once.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The fourth of five, and the only one that is a nationality.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chīnī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{chīnī}, and then \emph{chāy}, which you have had for a long time now
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\hi{आशीर्वाद}}, then say \emph{mez}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{चीनी} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}sugar\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sabzī]{\hi{सब्ज़ी} (sabzī) — a vegetable, vegetables}

\label{lesson:HI-C52-vegetable}



\begin{quote}
Name the 4 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{सब्ज़ी}}
\textbf{\hi{सब्ज़ी}} (\emph{sabzī}) — \textquotedblleft{}a vegetable, vegetables\textquotedblright{}.

A Persian word: \emph{sabz} means 'green', and \emph{-ī} turns an adjective into a noun. \hi{सब्ज़ी} is 'greenery' — the green things, taken together.

You have met this suffix already without being told: \hi{ख़ुशी} (\emph{khushī}), 'happiness', is \emph{khush}, 'pleased', with the same \emph{-ī} on the end. One ending, two words, both Persian.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The fifth of five. The kitchen is stocked.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sabzī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sabzī}, then \emph{dāl}, then \emph{chāval} — say the shelf in order
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{praṇām}, then say \emph{miṭhāī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{सब्ज़ी} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a vegetable, vegetables\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
